Custom JavaScript renderers

To use a custom JavaScript renderer, pass the renderer callback as the third argument to {@link vis.Create Create}, instead of a built-in renderer settings object. When a source snapshot is available, the callback runs when your script calls {@link Visualization#Draw Draw}. It receives the drawing context gr, the drawing rectangle x, y, w, h, and a data object containing the source's current measurements.

Numeric source data is passed to JavaScript renderer callbacks through reusable typed arrays such as Float32Array. Source-specific scalar metadata may also be present.

```js include('docs/Flags.js'); const visual = vis.Create(VisSourceType.PeakMeter, null, (gr, x, y, w, h, data) => { const level = data.levels[0]; gr.FillSolidRect(x, y, level * w, h, 0xff66ccaa); }); function on_paint(gr) { const w = window.Width, h = window.Height; gr.FillSolidRect(0, 0, w, h, 0xff101010); if (w > 0 && h > 0) visual.Draw(gr, 0, 0, w, h); } setInterval(() => window.Repaint(), 33); ```

Peak Meter provides one normalized level in data.levels; read it as data.levels[0] and multiply it by the rectangle width to obtain the bar width. The source already handles measurement and smoothing.

This is a complete script. JavaScript callback renderers can use both {@link GdiGraphics GDI} and {@link D2DGraphics Direct2D} drawing methods appropriate to the current graphics context. The callback runs on the drawing thread, not on the audio-analysis thread.

Passing a callback replaces only the renderer. The selected native source is still the same source described above, so its source runtime properties remain available on the returned object. For example, a custom Spectrum callback can still read or change Bands, FftSize, and the other Spectrum source properties. Built-in renderer properties such as ColorMode or Gap do not apply because the callback performs the drawing itself.

Values that conceptually represent a single number or boolean state still use one-element typed arrays—for example, the Peak Meter clipping flag is read as data.clipped[0]. Spectrogram also exposes scalar metadata describing its history ring.

Data lifetime: the visualization owns and reuses these buffers. Their contents are refreshed before a drawing callback when new analysis data is available; a source-size change can replace a buffer. Treat them as the current source state rather than permanent snapshots. Read the values you need during the callback; if you need to preserve a particular frame for later use, copy the relevant data into your own storage.

The sections below describe the callback data for each source. Unless marked as a complete script, each snippet replaces only the renderer callback body shown above. Source settings remain in the second argument; analyzed data is provided through data.

Waveform data

FieldTypeMeaning
lineFloat32ArrayResampled center trace, with signed amplitudes approximately from −1 to 1.
minFloat32ArrayMinimum PCM amplitude observed in each corresponding interval.
maxFloat32ArrayMaximum PCM amplitude observed in each corresponding interval.

The three arrays have the same length. The min/max envelope retains excursions that a single resampled point might miss, especially at narrow display widths. The following callback draws the center trace: sample index selects X; amplitude +1 maps to the top, 0 to the center and −1 to the bottom.

```js const { line } = data; if (line.length < 2) return; const amplitudeY = value => y + (1 - value) * h / 2; for (let i = 1; i < line.length; ++i) { const x0 = x + (i - 1) * w / (line.length - 1); const x1 = x + i * w / (line.length - 1); gr.DrawLine(x0, amplitudeY(line[i - 1]), x1, amplitudeY(line[i]), 1, 0xff66ccaa); } ```

Sample: JS - Waveform.js — draws both the resampled line and its min/max envelope.

Spectrum data

FieldTypeMeaning
levelsFloat32ArrayCurrent normalized magnitude for each frequency band. The array length is bands.
peaksFloat32ArrayHeld peak for each corresponding frequency band. The array length is bands.

Both arrays use the source's minDb/maxDb range on a normalized 0–1 scale; levels and peaks are capped at 0.98. The same index refers to the same frequency band in both arrays.

```js const { levels, peaks } = data; if (!levels.length) return; const bandWidth = w / levels.length; for (let i = 0; i < levels.length; ++i) { const left = x + i * bandWidth; const height = levels[i] * h; const peakY = y + (1 - peaks[i]) * h; gr.FillSolidRect(left, y + h - height, bandWidth, height, 0xff66ccaa); gr.DrawLine(left, peakY, left + bandWidth, peakY, 1, 0xffffffff); } ```

Sample: JS - Spectrum.js — draws both levels and held peaks.

Peak Meter data

FieldTypeMeaning
levelsFloat32Array(1)Current level, normalized to 0–1 over the configured minDb/maxDb range.
peaksFloat32Array(1)Held maximum on the same normalized meter scale.
clippedFloat32Array(1)Numeric clipping flag: element 0 is 1 while clipping is detected or retained by clipHoldMs, otherwise 0.

Read element 0 from each array. The clipping flag is separate from the meter scale and should be treated as an on/off state.

```js const level = data.levels[0]; // 0..1, current bar position. const peak = data.peaks[0]; // 0..1, held marker. const clipping = data.clipped[0] !== 0; gr.FillSolidRect(x, y, level * w, h, clipping ? 0xffff6655 : 0xff66ccaa); const peakX = x + peak * (w - 1); gr.DrawLine(peakX, y, peakX, y + h, 1, 0xffffffff); ```

Sample: JS - Peak Meter.js — shows the level, held peak and clipping lamp.

VU Meter data

FieldTypeMeaning
levelsFloat32Array(1)Current VU position, normalized to 0–1 over the source's minVu/maxVu scale.
peaksFloat32Array(1)Held VU marker on the same normalized scale.

Unlike the Peak Meter, these values describe the slower VU measurement rather than a peak-based dBFS level, and there is no clipping field. To draw a 0 VU reference mark, map zero with (0 - minVu) / (maxVu - minVu); the current reading is already normalized.

```js const vu = data.levels[0]; const held = data.peaks[0]; const minVu = -20, maxVu = 3; // Source defaults; use your configured range. const zeroVu = (0 - minVu) / (maxVu - minVu); gr.FillSolidRect(x, y, vu * w, h, 0xff66ccaa); const zeroX = x + zeroVu * (w - 1); const heldX = x + held * (w - 1); gr.DrawLine(zeroX, y, zeroX, y + h, 1, 0xff888888); gr.DrawLine(heldX, y, heldX, y + h, 1, 0xffffffff); ```

Sample: JS - VU Meter.js — uses both VU values.

Spectrogram data

Unlike the other sources, the spectrogram supplies a history of FFT columns, not merely one recent set of values. That history is kept in a circular buffer: older physical slots are reused as new audio arrives. The callback reports the data plus the information needed to reconstruct its chronological order.

FieldTypeMeaning
columnsFloat32ArrayLinear FFT magnitudes, stored column-major: one entire spectrum per physical history slot.
fftBinsnumberNumber of FFT magnitude values in each column.
sampleRatenumberCurrent audio sample rate in Hz, needed to turn bin positions into frequencies.
capacityColumnsnumberTotal number of physical column slots allocated in the history ring.
validColumnsnumberNumber of populated slots, from zero up to capacityColumns.
nextColumnnumberPhysical slot where the next FFT column will be written; not the newest column.
fullbooleanSignals that the retained history has been rebuilt and a cached display may need a complete redraw.

An FFT bin is one frequency measurement. The bins run from zero frequency to half the sample rate (the Nyquist frequency); adjacent bins are separated by sampleRate / (2 × (fftBins − 1)) hertz.

Read a magnitude using columns[column * fftBins + bin]. While the ring is not full, populated columns begin at physical slot 0. Once full, the oldest physical column is at nextColumn and the newest is (nextColumn - 1 + capacityColumns) % capacityColumns. Use validColumns when deciding how much history to show; do not assume unpopulated slots contain valid audio.

Start with a history of one frequency: this callback plots the FFT bin nearest 1000 Hz from oldest to newest. Convert its linear magnitude to decibels with 20 × log10(magnitude), then map the configured dB range to 0–1. The small positive floor avoids taking the logarithm of zero. Use your source settings if they differ from the defaults shown.

```js const { columns, fftBins, sampleRate, capacityColumns, validColumns, nextColumn } = data; if (!validColumns || fftBins < 2 || sampleRate <= 0) return; // One FFT bin near 1000 Hz; fftBins includes zero and the Nyquist bin. const bin = Math.min(fftBins - 1, Math.round(1000 * 2 * (fftBins - 1) / sampleRate)); const minDb = -78, maxDb = 0, gain = 1; // Source defaults. const oldest = validColumns < capacityColumns ? 0 : nextColumn; const columnWidth = w / validColumns; for (let n = 0; n < validColumns; ++n) { const slot = (oldest + n) % capacityColumns; const magnitude = columns[slot * fftBins + bin] * gain; const db = 20 * Math.log10(Math.max(magnitude, 1e-12)); const level = Math.max(0, Math.min(1, (db - minDb) / (maxDb - minDb))); const height = level * h; gr.FillSolidRect(x + n * columnWidth, y + h - height, columnWidth, height, 0xff66ccaa); } ```

This example redraws the available history and stretches it across the rectangle. A full spectrogram repeats the magnitude-to-intensity conversion for multiple frequencies and maps intensity to color. The linked sample adds a frequency scale, a fixed scrolling speed, and a cached bitmap updated only for new columns.

Sample: JS - Spectrogram.js — implements the ring mapping, palette, offscreen image and incremental updates.

Vectorscope data

left and right describe the stereo waveform used to draw the vectorscope trace. Optional relativeBands serves a different purpose: it gives a custom renderer simple signals with which to animate color, size, glow, zoom, or other effect parameters in response to the music. It follows changes within three broad frequency regions relative to their usual levels, rather than reporting absolute volume.

FieldTypeMeaning
leftFloat32ArraySigned PCM samples from the selected left channel, approximately −1 to 1.
rightFloat32ArraySigned PCM samples from the selected right channel, approximately −1 to 1.
relativeBandsFloat32Array(6), when enabledMusic-reactive controls in the order bass, mid, treb, bass_att, mid_att, treb_att. Values are non-negative ratios relative to each band's long-term level; 1 represents its usual activity. See Optional relative band controls below.

The left and right arrays have equal length, and their entries at index i belong to the same stereo audio frame. The example draws one point per pair around the rectangle center. Positive vertical amplitude moves upward, so subtract it from the center Y coordinate. Connect adjacent pairs only if you intend to show a continuous trace.

```js const { left, right } = data; const radius = Math.max(0, Math.min(w, h) / 2 - 1); for (let i = 0; i < left.length; ++i) { const sx = (left[i] - right[i]) / 2; const sy = (left[i] + right[i]) / 2; const px = x + w / 2 + sx * radius; const py = y + h / 2 - sy * radius; gr.FillSolidRect(px, py, 1, 1, 0xff66ccaa); } ```

Sample: JS - Vectorscope.js — visualizes the paired channels and their stereo axes.

Optional relative band controls

Set relativeBandAnalysis: true in the Vectorscope source settings to obtain relativeBands. The engine analyzes the two selected channels separately and combines their frequency magnitudes, so opposite-polarity stereo signals do not cancel out as they could in a mono mix. It also maintains the reference levels and attack/release smoothing; your renderer can use the resulting controls directly.

ControlApproximate frequency rangeSmoothed control
bass0–200 Hzbass_att
mid200–4000 Hzmid_att
treb4000–20000 Hztreb_att

A value of 1 is the band's usual level; values above 1 indicate stronger activity. Sustained activity gradually becomes part of that reference, so a band held at a consistently high absolute level tends back toward 1 instead of remaining permanently above it. These are relative controls, not dBFS readings or beat-detection events. The reference adapts quickly for about 1.67 seconds after a reset, then more slowly. Very quiet input uses the neutral value 1, so it should not be interpreted as an absolute silence detector.

Keep durationMs separate from {@link vis.UpdateIntervalMs}: the former selects the PCM window, while the latter requests how often analysis runs. Changing the window can change the timing of the band response. Sources with the same selected channel pair and duration share the reference history. Stopped playback resets it; on pause, the retained PCM is still analyzed and the relative values can continue to change.

This complete JavaScript example draws three horizontal bars: bass, mid and treble from top to bottom. Each colored bar follows the immediate value; a white marker follows its smoothed counterpart, and a short gray tick marks the reference level 1. The callback uses only relativeBands, so it does not need to draw the stereo PCM trace.

```js include('docs/Flags.js'); const colors = [0xffff7766, 0xff77cc88, 0xff77aaff]; const bandsView = vis.Create(VisSourceType.Vectorscope, { relativeBandAnalysis: true }, (gr, x, y, w, h, data) => { const bands = data.relativeBands; const rowHeight = h / 3; for (let i = 0; i < 3; ++i) { const top = y + (i + 0.15) * rowHeight; const height = rowHeight * 0.7; // Display 0..2: the usual level (1) is halfway across. const current = Math.min(bands[i], 2) / 2; const smoothed = Math.min(bands[i + 3], 2) / 2; gr.FillSolidRect(x, top, current * w, height, colors[i]); const referenceX = Math.round(x + w / 2); gr.DrawLine(referenceX, top + height - 5, referenceX, top + height, 1, 0xff888888); // Reference level: 1. const markerX = Math.round(x + smoothed * (w - 1)); gr.DrawLine(markerX, top, markerX, top + height, 1, 0xffffffff); } }); function on_paint(gr) { const w = window.Width, h = window.Height; gr.FillSolidRect(0, 0, w, h, 0xff101010); if (w > 0 && h > 0) bandsView.Draw(gr, 0, 0, w, h); } setInterval(() => window.Repaint(), 33); ```

Indices 0–2 select bass, mid and treb; adding 3 selects the matching _att value. The display caps values at 2 only to keep the drawing inside the rectangle; the source data remains unchanged and may exceed 2. During playback, compare the colored bar with the white marker to see the smoothing. You can use the same values to control a shape's size or color instead of drawing bars.

JavaScript callbacks are useful for custom layouts, labels and geometry using familiar drawing operations. For effects that calculate a color for every pixel, a shader is another way to render the same native source.

Custom HLSL renderers

Use a custom HLSL renderer when you want to implement the visualization as a pixel shader. The native source still captures and analyzes the audio; your shader receives prepared source data and produces the pixels drawn by {@link Visualization#Draw Draw}.

Create it with {@link vis.CreateAsync vis.CreateAsync}. The third argument is a renderer object containing shader, in place of built-in renderer settings. Shader visualizations require {@link window.DrawMode} set to 1 (Direct2D). The returned object is a normal {@link Visualization}: source runtime properties remain available, while the shader defines the appearance.

The examples below build a Peak Meter shader from one analyzed audio value, then extend it with image passes.

1. Create a visualization that fills its rectangle

Start with a shader that ignores the audio and returns the same color for every pixel. The Peak Meter source is already selected here; its level will be used in step 3.

```js include('docs/Flags.js'); window.DrawMode = 1; // Shader visualizations require Direct2D. const shader = ` float4 main() : SV_Target { return float4(0.4, 0.9, 0.6, 1.0); }`; let visual = null; vis.CreateAsync(VisSourceType.PeakMeter, null, { shader }) .then(v => { visual = v; window.Repaint(); }) .catch(e => console.log("Visualization creation failed: " + e)); function on_paint(gr) { const w = window.Width, h = window.Height; gr.FillSolidRect(0, 0, w, h, 0xff101010); if (visual && w > 0 && h > 0) visual.Draw(gr, 0, 0, w, h); } setInterval(() => window.Repaint(), 33); // Request roughly 30 FPS presentation. ```

The HLSL entry point is main. It returns a float4 containing red, green, blue and alpha values; SV_Target marks that value as the output pixel color. Here every pixel receives the same opaque color.

The JavaScript string shader contains the GPU program, and { shader } is shorthand for a renderer object whose shader property contains that string. {@link vis.CreateAsync CreateAsync} compiles the shader off the panel UI thread and resolves to the visualization when it is ready. The repaint timer and {@link Visualization#Draw Draw} work the same way as with other visualizations.

For the next two steps, keep this JavaScript setup and replace only the HLSL inside the shader string, then reload the script.

2. Give each pixel a position

Next, use the current pixel position and the drawing size to produce a horizontal gradient.

```hlsl cbuffer Params : register(b0) { float2 viewportSize; }; struct PS { float4 clipSpacePos : SV_POSITION; float4 sceneSpacePos : SCENE_POS; }; float4 main(PS p) : SV_Target { float x = p.sceneSpacePos.x / max(viewportSize.x, 1.0); return float4(x, 0.4, 0.2, 1.0); } ```

The red component now increases from left to right. sceneSpacePos.xy is the local pixel position supplied to main; X increases rightward and Y downward. viewportSize is the drawing width and height supplied through the constant buffer at b0. Dividing X by the width gives a relative position from about 0 to 1.

A constant buffer is a group of values supplied by the host. register(b0) selects its binding slot; nothing is passed explicitly from JavaScript. SCENE_POS identifies the local-position input. SV_POSITION is also part of the shader input layout but is not used here.

This example declares only the first two floats of b0. The complete layout is listed in Source shader input reference.

3. Read one audio value

Now use the Peak Meter source data to turn the rectangle into a level meter.

```hlsl Texture2D Level : register(t0); cbuffer Params : register(b0) { float2 viewportSize; }; struct PS { float4 clipSpacePos : SV_POSITION; float4 sceneSpacePos : SCENE_POS; }; float4 main(PS p) : SV_Target { float level = Level.Load(int3(0, 0, 0)); float alpha = p.sceneSpacePos.x < level * viewportSize.x ? 1.0 : 0.0; return float4(0.4 * alpha, 0.9 * alpha, 0.6 * alpha, alpha); } ```

The Peak Meter source publishes its normalized level from 0 to 1 through a texture bound at t0. Texture2D<float> declares a texture containing floating-point values, and Load(int3(0, 0, 0)) reads its first value. The source already performs level detection and smoothing; the shader only turns that value into a bar width.

During playback, the green bar follows the current level. Pixels outside it return transparent black, revealing the background drawn by {@link module:Callbacks.on_paint on_paint}. Shader output uses premultiplied RGBA: multiply RGB by alpha whenever the output is transparent or partially transparent.

The three input mechanisms now have distinct roles: b0 provides values shared by the draw, SCENE_POS identifies the current pixel, and t0 supplies analyzed audio. Their HLSL names can change, but their bindings and layouts must match the selected source.

Other sources use the same creation and drawing setup with different texture layouts; see Source shader input reference. The following sections add image passes to this Peak Meter.

Shader pipeline

A single source shader is enough for many effects. To process its finished image, add post; to carry part of an image into later frames, add feedback. Each additional shader execution is called a pass. Both options work with all six sources, and you can use either one or both.

JSplitter connects the passes, creates the intermediate images, composites the source and maintains feedback history. You supply the shaders and their configuration; there is no need to copy the screen into a bitmap on every paint or maintain a pair of history images in JavaScript.

Adding a post pass

A post shader reads the completed image at t0. Its input is RGBA pixels, rather than the audio values used by the main shader. Declare Texture2D for that image and a SamplerState at s0 for filtered reads. The additional TEXEL_POS input provides coordinates for sampling the image. The following example swaps red and blue while keeping transparency unchanged.

Keep the Peak Meter shader from step 3 and replace its creation call with:

```js const colorPost = ` Texture2D InputImage : register(t0); SamplerState InputSampler : register(s0); struct PSInput { float4 clipSpacePos : SV_POSITION; float4 sceneSpacePos : SCENE_POS; float4 texelSpacePos : TEXEL_POS; }; float4 main(PSInput p) : SV_Target { float4 color = InputImage.SampleLevel(InputSampler, p.texelSpacePos.xy, 0); return float4(color.b, color.g, color.r, color.a); }`; vis.CreateAsync(VisSourceType.PeakMeter, null, { shader, post: colorPost }) .then(v => { visual = v; window.Repaint(); }) .catch(e => console.log("Visualization creation failed: " + e)); ```

SampleLevel() samples the image through s0; texelSpacePos.xy provides the corresponding input texture coordinates. Unlike an audio-texture Load(), this can interpolate between neighboring pixels. Returning the sampled color unchanged makes an image pass do nothing; here, only the output color channels change.

post accepts one pass or an array of one to four passes. They run in array order, and each reads the preceding pass's output. A post pass cannot read the original source or an earlier pass separately unless that information is carried through its input image.

Sample: Shader - Image Post.js demonstrates a complete visualization with an independent post effect.

Adding feedback

feedback reads the previously saved history at t0. It can fade, move or distort that image. JSplitter then draws the current source image over the result and saves the combined image as the next history. Post-processing, if present, runs after that save and never returns to the loop.

For simple fading trails, sample history and reduce its brightness. This pass also reads frameStep from b0: one history step in 60-Hz units, approximately 1 at 60 updates per second and 2 at 30. Using it in the exponent makes the fade account for elapsed time. The preceding viewportSize and time fields keep frameStep at the required fourth-float position, even though this shader does not use them.

```js const fadeFeedback = ` Texture2D InputImage : register(t0); SamplerState InputSampler : register(s0); cbuffer ImageConstants : register(b0) { float2 viewportSize; float time; float frameStep; }; struct PSInput { float4 clipSpacePos : SV_POSITION; float4 sceneSpacePos : SCENE_POS; float4 texelSpacePos : TEXEL_POS; }; float4 main(PSInput p) : SV_Target { float4 history = InputImage.SampleLevel(InputSampler, p.texelSpacePos.xy, 0); history.rgb *= pow(0.96, frameStep); return history; }`; ```

Use fadeFeedback as feedback in the creation call. This keeps 96% of the history color per 60 Hz time unit, gradually darkening older traces. The current meter bar is added by the engine after the fade; you do not draw it again in the feedback shader.

```js // Use this renderer object in the preceding creation call: const renderer = { shader, feedback: fadeFeedback, post: colorPost }; ```

Source transparency matters: an opaque source covers the transformed history. The meter shader from step 3 returns transparent pixels outside the bar, so older, fading levels remain visible when the current level falls. The source is composited over history using its alpha; it is not automatically added to the previous RGB values.

Each visualization owns its own history, initially black. By default that background is opaque. Set feedbackTransparent: true to start with transparent black and retain meaningful alpha in the accumulated image, for example when the visualization should reveal the panel beneath it. In every pass, return premultiplied RGBA: when you change alpha, keep RGB multiplied by that alpha too.

Sample: Shader - Feedback and Two Posts.js combines a history effect with two ordered post passes.

Feedback update rate

By default, every {@link Visualization#Draw Draw} call advances feedback history once. Set feedbackIntervalMs to request a different history cadence. The source and feedback then advance together only when a history step is due; between steps, the last completed history is shown through the post passes.

```js // Add this property to a renderer that already has a feedback pass: const renderer = { shader, feedback: fadeFeedback, post: colorPost, feedbackIntervalMs: 1000 / 30 // Request about 30 history steps per second. }; ```

This setting does not create a timer. A history step can run only when the script calls {@link Visualization#Draw Draw}; repaint often enough to support the requested cadence. Missed steps are skipped rather than replayed with old audio. Post shaders can still animate on every repaint even when history is unchanged.

time describes the animation clock, while frameStep describes one rendering step. For per-draw feedback and all post passes, frameStep is the elapsed draw interval multiplied by 60, clamped to 0.001–6. With a positive feedbackIntervalMs, feedback and the non-spectrogram source shader instead receive the configured interval multiplied by 0.06, clamped to 0.001–60. Spectrogram's main shader has its own constant layout and no frameStep field.

To turn a rate expressed per second into a per-step change, multiply it by frameStep / 60. For a time-scaled formula designed around 30 FPS, use frameStep / 2 as the step multiplier. The fading example uses an exponential factor so the intended fade rate follows step time.

This does not make every effect independent of FPS: repeated resampling, source opacity, and nonlinear operations can still change the accumulated image. Increasing only the repaint rate does not increase a separately limited history rate.

Change {@link Visualization#FeedbackIntervalMs FeedbackIntervalMs} on an existing shader visualization to adjust this cadence without recompiling or clearing history. The next eligible {@link Visualization#Draw Draw} starts the new schedule. It accepts 0 or a finite number from 1 to 1000 milliseconds, including fractional values; a positive value requires a feedback pass. Assigning the same value keeps the schedule intact; assigning 0 returns to one history step per draw. Audio analysis and the animation clock are preserved. The setter neither requests a repaint nor bypasses pause or resize freezes.

```js visual.FeedbackIntervalMs = 1000 / 120; // Fixed history step at 120 FPS. const interval = visual.FeedbackIntervalMs; // Read the current setting. visual.FeedbackIntervalMs = 0; // Return to per-Draw history. // The repaint timer is separate; keep it fast enough for the desired cadence. ```

The image-pass interface

Feedback and post shaders use the same image interface, shown in full in fadeFeedback. Declare the inputs needed by your shader; colorPost does not need the constant buffer. Their bindings have different meanings from the main source shader's bindings:

InputContents
t0 / s0The image being processed and its sampler. Feedback receives previous history; the first post receives the completed current image; later posts receive the preceding post output.
b0: float2 viewportSizeCurrent output width and height in pixels.
b0: float timeAnimation time in seconds since the first usable draw; it restarts when the underlying Direct2D device changes.
b0: float frameStepTime step in 60 Hz frame units. Here it is the fourth float, in place of the source shader's element count.
sceneSpacePos.xyLocal output pixel position; divide by viewportSize for a logical position in the drawing rectangle.
texelSpacePos.xyCoordinates for sampling the preceding image. Use these for a direct image read.
t1–t3 / s1–s3Optional image files attached to this pass, described below. These are not the main shader's audio textures.

Image passes do not receive the source's audio textures or arbitrary JavaScript uniforms. Keep audio-driven drawing in the main shader, or encode information needed by later passes in the image it produces.

When changing sample coordinates: logical output coordinates and input texture coordinates need not cover the same 0–1 range. In a chain, an input image may occupy only part of its backing texture. Use texelSpacePos for input sampling and map any logical offsets into that coordinate space; do not assume that replacing it with sceneSpacePos / viewportSize always reads the same pixel.

Adding image files to a pass

To use a noise texture, mask or other image alongside history, replace that pass's HLSL string with an object containing shader and textures. The preceding image remains at t0; one to three files bind in array order at t1 through t3, with matching samplers at s1 through s3.

This example applies a grayscale opacity mask after the earlier color post effect. Supply an existing mask file and adjust the path: white keeps the image, black makes it transparent. The shader stretches the mask over the drawing rectangle using local output coordinates, while reading the preceding image with its own texture coordinates. Multiplying all four color components preserves premultiplied alpha.

```js const texturedPost = ` Texture2D InputImage : register(t0); SamplerState InputSampler : register(s0); Texture2D Mask : register(t1); SamplerState MaskSampler : register(s1); cbuffer ImageConstants : register(b0) { float2 viewportSize; }; struct PSInput { float4 clipSpacePos : SV_POSITION; float4 sceneSpacePos : SCENE_POS; float4 texelSpacePos : TEXEL_POS; }; float4 main(PSInput p) : SV_Target { float4 color = InputImage.SampleLevel(InputSampler, p.texelSpacePos.xy, 0); float2 maskUV = p.sceneSpacePos.xy / max(viewportSize, 1.0); float opacity = Mask.SampleLevel(MaskSampler, saturate(maskUV), 0).r; return color * opacity; }`; // Use this renderer object in the earlier CreateAsync call. const renderer = { shader, feedback: fadeFeedback, post: [colorPost, { shader: texturedPost, textures: ["images/mask.png"] // Supply an existing image file. }] }; ```

The object form is available for feedback and for each post pass. Attach an image to the pass that samples it: textures are not shared automatically between passes, and the main shader uses its source-defined audio bindings.

Paths follow the usual script image-path rules. JSplitter reads and decodes the files during asynchronous creation and retains those pixels. If the graphics device is recreated, its textures are uploaded again from the retained data without rereading the files. Create a new visualization to load changed image files. During rendering they are fixed inputs, not additional history images. Define wrapping explicitly in HLSL, for example by applying frac() to the coordinates used for an auxiliary texture.

Shader renderer settings

The third argument to {@link vis.CreateAsync CreateAsync} accepts the following shader renderer settings. See {@link VisualizationShaderRenderer} for the complete reference.

SettingRuntimeDefaultDescription
shader—RequiredNon-empty HLSL text or compiled DXBC. Generates the source image.
feedback—OmittedOne image pass, or null to omit it. Transforms saved history before the source is composited.
post—OmittedOne image pass, an array of 1–4 passes, or null. Processes only the displayed result.
feedbackIntervalMs{@link Visualization#FeedbackIntervalMs FeedbackIntervalMs}00 for every draw, or a finite number from 1 to 1000 ms, including fractional values. A positive value requires feedback.
feedbackTransparent—falseUse transparent history instead of an opaque black background; true requires feedback.
stopOnPause—falseFreeze the completed image, including post effects, when playback is paused.

An image pass may be a direct HLSL/DXBC value or a {@link VisualizationImagePass} object with shader and optional textures. HLSL and DXBC can be mixed within a pipeline; compilation options are covered at the end of this article.

Pause, resizing and history lifetime

With the default stopOnPause: false, shaders continue to run on pause using the source's retained audio data; feedback can keep evolving. Set it to true to display the last completed image until playback resumes. This freezes rendering, not native audio analysis. In either case, the script remains responsible for requesting repaints.

For a visualization with feedback, while the drawing size is changing JSplitter temporarily scales a snapshot of the last completed image. Once the size settles, it resizes the saved history once and resumes the pipeline. Without feedback, an active source/post pipeline renders directly at the new size. A paused, frozen image is simply scaled without reprocessing it.

Feedback supports drawing areas up to 4096 pixels per side and 4,194,304 pixels in total. History belongs to the visualization instance; creating another instance starts a new history, and a graphics-device change resets it. Switching between panel and bitmap graphics on the same Direct2D device preserves history.

If a Waveform or Vectorscope source temporarily has no PCM, its source image is not added to feedback. Existing history can still advance through feedback and post, which lets trails continue between tracks. This is separate from the paused-playback behavior above.

Injecting a bitmap into feedback history

Use {@link Visualization#InjectFeedback InjectFeedback} when an image should become part of recursive feedback rather than a normal overlay. The visualization must have a feedback pass.

```js // 'visual' was created with vis.CreateAsync() and feedback enabled. const w = 640, h = 128; const bitmap = d2d.CreateImage(w, h); const bg = bitmap.GetGraphics(); try { bg.DrawString('Now playing', d2d.Font('Segoe UI', 30), 0xffffffff, 20, 20, w - 40, 64); } finally { bitmap.ReleaseGraphics(bg); } visual.InjectFeedback(bitmap); ```

{@link Visualization#InjectFeedback InjectFeedback} copies the bitmap to the GPU and queues it for the next feedback-history update. At that update, JSplitter processes the previous history through the feedback pass, composites the current source image, then alpha-composites the injected bitmap and saves the result. Any post pass runs afterwards for presentation.

If feedbackIntervalMs postpones the next history update, the bitmap remains pending until that update occurs. Calling {@link Visualization#InjectFeedback InjectFeedback} again before then replaces the pending bitmap. The method does not request a repaint or force an early history update.

The argument must be a {@link D2DBitmap} on the same D2D device as the visualization; GDI bitmaps are not accepted. The dimensions must not exceed 4096 pixels per side or 4,194,304 pixels in total. Injected images are scaled to the feedback surface, so use a suitable aspect ratio. To draw graphics that must stay outside feedback history, draw them after {@link Visualization#Draw visual.Draw} in {@link module:Callbacks.on_paint on_paint}.

Preset hand-off: Shader - MilkDrop ALL.js captures the outgoing preset into an offscreen D2D bitmap and injects it once into the incoming preset. The incoming feedback shader then controls how that image is distorted and faded; no second visualization is kept running for a screen-space crossfade.

Complete MilkDrop example and preset browser

Standalone sample: Shader - MilkDrop 0101.js contains a complete, runnable port in a single file. It defines the Vectorscope source settings and all three HLSL stages (shader, feedback and post) before passing them directly to {@link vis.CreateAsync CreateAsync}. It is a good starting point for studying or modifying the full pipeline without loading separate preset files.

Preset browser: Shader - MilkDrop ALL.js discovers readable JavaScript preset files in samples/vis/MilkDrop, including 0101. Each numbered file contains commented HLSL strings and a factory that returns its source settings and renderer object for the selected FPS. The browser offers 30, 60 and 120 FPS buttons and accepts integer targets from 30 to 1000; these are repaint requests, not a guaranteed rendering rate. Add another four-digit .js file and reload the panel to make it available.

The browser loads trusted preset files through {@link include include}, compiles their shaders with {@link vis.CreateAsync CreateAsync}, hands the outgoing frame to the incoming feedback via {@link Visualization#InjectFeedback InjectFeedback}, and displays live native cache statistics.

Changing FPS preserves the active visualization and its history. Most presets advance history on every draw; a preset that opts into fixed cadence through feedbackIntervalMs, such as 0176, has its factory interval re-evaluated and applied through {@link Visualization#FeedbackIntervalMs FeedbackIntervalMs}. Audio analysis cadence and the PCM window remain separate from display FPS. Both samples use the public visualization API and need no MilkDrop-specific native API.

Source shader input reference

The main shader receives the selected source's analysis data through textures t0..t2 and its drawing constants through b0. The snippets below show the smallest useful reads for each source; the linked samples contain complete shaders.

For non-spectrogram sources, b0 starts with this layout:

```hlsl cbuffer VisConstants : register(b0) { float2 viewportSize; float time; float sourceCount; float frameStep; }; ```

The fourth float is the number of source elements. Name it pointCount or bandCount when that makes the shader clearer. frameStep is optional and uses 60 Hz frame units. The field names are yours to choose; the order and types are not.

Audio textures use R32F, so declare them as Texture2D<float> and read exact values with Load():

```hlsl Texture2D Input : register(t0); float value = Input.Load(int3(i, 0, 0)).r; ```

For one-row textures, index i selects the source element and the final zero selects mip level 0. No sampler is needed for these reads. sceneSpacePos.xy is the current pixel position inside the rectangle passed to {@link Visualization#Draw Draw}.

Waveform

t0 contains the recent waveform as signed PCM values. A horizontal pixel can select one source sample like this:

```hlsl Texture2D Samples : register(t0); int count = max((int)pointCount, 1); int i = clamp((int)(input.sceneSpacePos.x / max(viewportSize.x, 1.0) * count), 0, count - 1); float amplitude = Samples.Load(int3(i, 0, 0)).r; ```
InputLayoutContents
t0pointCount × 1 R32FSigned resampled waveform values, approximately −1 to 1.
b0 countpointCountNumber of valid waveform samples.

Map +1 to the top, 0 to the center and −1 to the bottom. The shader texture contains the center trace only; the min/max envelope exposed to JavaScript callbacks is not uploaded to HLSL.

Sample: Shader - Waveform.js.

Spectrum

t0 and t1 use the same band index:

```hlsl Texture2D Levels : register(t0); Texture2D Peaks : register(t1); float level = Levels.Load(int3(i, 0, 0)).r; float peak = Peaks.Load(int3(i, 0, 0)).r; ```
InputLayoutContents
t0bandCount × 1 R32FCurrent normalized FFT-band levels.
t1bandCount × 1 R32FHeld peaks for the same bands.
b0 countbandCountNumber of valid bands in both textures.

Values use the source's minDb/maxDb range on a normalized 0–1 scale and are capped at 0.98. Source frequency settings define what each band represents; the shader decides only how to place those bands on screen.

Sample: Shader - Spectrum.js.

Peak Meter

The meter exposes its current level, held peak and clipping state as three 1×1 textures:

```hlsl Texture2D Level : register(t0); Texture2D Peak : register(t1); Texture2D Clip : register(t2); float level = Level.Load(int3(0, 0, 0)).r; float peak = Peak.Load(int3(0, 0, 0)).r; bool clipped = Clip.Load(int3(0, 0, 0)).r != 0.0; ```
InputLayoutContents
t01 × 1 R32FCurrent normalized level, 0–1.
t11 × 1 R32FHeld peak position, 0–1.
t21 × 1 R32FNumeric clipping flag: 0 or 1.
b0 countsourceCount = 1Single meter value set.

The source already applies its attack/release, peak hold and clipping hold behavior. The shader only renders the resulting values.

Sample: Shader - Peak Meter.js.

VU Meter

VU Meter uses the same first two slots for its current and held readings:

```hlsl Texture2D VU : register(t0); Texture2D Hold : register(t1); float current = VU.Load(int3(0, 0, 0)).r; float marker = Hold.Load(int3(0, 0, 0)).r; ```
InputLayoutContents
t01 × 1 R32FCurrent normalized VU reading over the configured minVu..maxVu range.
t11 × 1 R32FHeld VU marker on the same normalized scale.
t21 × 1 R32FReserved auxiliary slot containing zero; VU Meter does not expose clipping.
b0 countsourceCount = 1Single meter value set.

The source performs the VU measurement and smoothing. A 0 VU reference tick is a display convention, not another input value.

Sample: Shader - VU Meter.js.

Spectrogram

Spectrogram is the exception to the one-row texture layout. t0 is a 2D circular history: X is time and Y is frequency, with high frequencies at the top. The shader receives the ring position in an extended b0:

```hlsl Texture2D History : register(t0); cbuffer VisConstants : register(b0) { float2 viewportSize; float time; float sourceCount; // 1 float textureWidth; float textureHeight; float nextColumn; // Next physical write slot. float validColumns; float scrollPixels; float reserved0; float reserved1; float reserved2; float4 reservedColor; }; ```

For a full ring, display column x maps to the physical texture by wrapping from nextColumn:

```hlsl int width = max((int)textureWidth, 1); int height = max((int)textureHeight, 1); int x = clamp((int)(input.sceneSpacePos.x / max(viewportSize.x, 1.0) * width), 0, width - 1); int row = clamp((int)(input.sceneSpacePos.y / max(viewportSize.y, 1.0) * height), 0, height - 1); int physicalX = ((int)nextColumn + x) % width; float level = History.Load(int3(physicalX, row, 0)).r; ```
InputLayoutContents
t02D R32F history textureCircular timeline of normalized spectral intensities. Columns are time slots; rows are frequency cells.
b016 floatsViewport, time, texture dimensions, ring position, valid-column count and fractional scroll position.

Texture values are already normalized: 0 corresponds to minDb and 1 to maxDb. Before the ring fills, only validColumns slots contain history; the complete sample handles the partial-ring case and scrollPixels for smooth scrolling. One display-history column represents 20 ms on the fixed 50 px/s display timeline, independently of the source's columnIntervalMs.

Sample: Shader - Spectrogram.js.

Vectorscope

t0 and t1 contain synchronized left/right PCM samples. Read the same index from both, then convert the pair to vectorscope coordinates:

```hlsl Texture2D Left : register(t0); Texture2D Right : register(t1); float L = Left.Load(int3(i, 0, 0)).r; float R = Right.Load(int3(i, 0, 0)).r; float2 xy = float2((L - R) * 0.5, (L + R) * 0.5); ```
InputLayoutContents
t0pointCount × 1 R32FSigned PCM samples from the selected left channel, approximately −1 to 1.
t1pointCount × 1 R32FCorresponding samples from the selected right channel.
t29 × 1 R32F when enabledRelative and absolute bass/mid/treble analysis; see below.
b0 countpointCountNumber of synchronized stereo sample pairs.

With relativeBandAnalysis: true, t2 is also bound:

```hlsl Texture2D Bands : register(t2); float bass = Bands.Load(int3(0, 0, 0)).r; float mid = Bands.Load(int3(1, 0, 0)).r; float treb = Bands.Load(int3(2, 0, 0)).r; float bassAtt = Bands.Load(int3(3, 0, 0)).r; ```

Indices 0–2 are the immediate bass, mid and treb levels relative to their long-term averages; 3–5 are the attack/release-smoothed versions. A value of 1 matches the adaptive long-term reference level, and the relative values are not clamped to 0–1. Indices 6–8 contain the corresponding immediate absolute magnitude sums. This option belongs to the Vectorscope source settings, not the shader renderer.

A pixel shader that plots many PCM points may be considerably more expensive than the built-in Vectorscope renderer because each output pixel can examine multiple source samples.

Sample: Shader - Vectorscope.js.

Compilation and shader reuse

For normal use, pass HLSL directly to {@link vis.CreateAsync CreateAsync}. JSplitter compiles each HLSL stage asynchronously and caches the resulting DXBC; no explicit compilation is required.

Automatic compilation and shader cache

{@link vis.ShaderTarget} selects the shader profile used by {@link vis.CreateAsync CreateAsync}, and {@link vis.ShaderFlags} selects the compiler flags. The defaults are ps_4_0 and 0x8008 (optimization level 3 with row-major matrix packing). Each creation call captures these settings for all of its HLSL stages; later changes affect only subsequent calls.

Compiled HLSL is stored in a process-wide, in-memory LRU cache shared by JSplitter panels. Cache entries are keyed by the exact HLSL source text, shader profile and compiler flags. Each stage is looked up separately, so identical HLSL can reuse the same entry across stages and panels. The cache is discarded when foobar2000 exits.

{@link vis.ShaderCacheMaxEntries} (default 128, allowed 0–4096) and {@link vis.ShaderCacheMaxBytes} (default 16 MiB, allowed 0–1 GiB) limit the cache independently. Setting either limit to zero disables caching; lowering a limit immediately evicts least-recently-used entries as needed. The limits are process-wide and are not saved across restarts. {@link vis.ShaderCacheMaxBytes} measures approximate CPU memory retained for source text, profiles and bytecode, not GPU memory.

{@link vis.ShaderCacheStats} returns a fresh {@link ShaderCacheStats} snapshot:

```js const { Entries, Bytes, Hits, Misses, Evictions } = vis.ShaderCacheStats; console.log(`HLSL cache: ${Entries}/${vis.ShaderCacheMaxEntries} entries, ` + `${Bytes}/${vis.ShaderCacheMaxBytes} bytes; ${Hits} hits, ` + `${Misses} misses, ${Evictions} evictions`); ```

The cache is used only by automatic HLSL compilation in {@link vis.CreateAsync CreateAsync}. Precompiled DXBC bypasses it, and {@link d2d.Compile} / {@link d2d.CompileAsync} do not use it and compile on every call. {@link vis.ShaderCacheStats} therefore reports only automatic {@link vis.CreateAsync CreateAsync} compilation. Cache limits affect future reuse only; visualizations that are already running are unchanged.

Explicit compilation and DXBC reuse

Use {@link d2d.CompileAsync d2d.CompileAsync} when you want to compile HLSL explicitly and keep the resulting DXBC for reuse. It returns the same {@link D2DCompileInfo} result as synchronous {@link d2d.Compile d2d.Compile}, but runs without blocking the calling JavaScript thread. Both methods default to entry point main and profile ps_4_0, and take their own profile and flags arguments.

```js async function createCompiledMeter(hlsl) { const compiled = await d2d.CompileAsync(hlsl); if (compiled.Error) throw new Error(compiled.Error); return vis.CreateAsync(VisSourceType.PeakMeter, null, { shader: compiled.Code }); } ```

{@link vis.CreateAsync CreateAsync} accepts precompiled DXBC as a Uint8Array or ArrayBuffer anywhere an HLSL shader stage is accepted, so HLSL and DXBC stages can be mixed in the same pipeline. Supported bytecode profiles are ps_4_0, ps_4_1 and ps_5_0; the selected profile must be supported by the GPU and the shader must follow the same source or image-pass input contract as HLSL.

An HLSL compiler error from {@link d2d.CompileAsync d2d.CompileAsync} is returned in {@link D2DCompileInfo#Error D2DCompileInfo.Error}; other setup or task failures can reject the Promise. Synchronous {@link d2d.Compile d2d.Compile} is also available, but a large compilation can block the UI. Compatible DXBC produced by an external HLSL compiler can be used in the same way.

The runnable visualization samples are in component/samples/vis and are available through the vis sample category in the panel configurator. The links in this article open their corresponding source files in the generated API documentation.
